The '''Communications and Information Services Corps''' ('''CIS''') ({{langx|ga|An Cór Seirbhísí Cumarsáide agus Eolais}}) – formerly the Army Corps of Signals – is one of the combat support corps of the [[Defence Forces (Ireland)|Irish Defence Forces]], the military of [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. It is responsible for the installation, maintenance and operation of [[Communications system|communications]] and [[information system]]s for the command, control and administration of the Defence Forces, and the facilitation of accurate, [[Real-time data|real-time]] sharing of intelligence between the [[Irish Army|Army]], [[Naval Service (Ireland)|Naval Service]] and [[Air Corps (Ireland)|Air Corps]] branches at home and overseas.<ref name="cis 1">{{cite web|title=Communications and Information Service Corps|url=http://www.military.ie/en/army/organisation/army-corps/cis/|publisher=Department of Defence|access-date=5 June 2015}}</ref>

The CIS Corps is headquartered at [[McKee Barracks]], [[Dublin]], and comes under the command of an officer of [[Colonel]] rank, known as the Director of CIS Corps.<ref>{{cite news|title=Telecoms minefield for Army in Liberia|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/business/telecoms-minefield-for-army-in-liberia-1.420214|access-date=7 July 2015|publisher=The Irish Times|date=4 March 2005}}</ref>

==Mission==
[[File:Cis intel curragh offices,co.kildare.PNG|thumbnail|Members of the Defence Forces CIS at the [[Curragh Camp]], [[County Kildare]]]]
Formerly the Army Corps of Signals, the Communications and Information Services Corps is responsible for the development and operation of Information Technology and Telecommunications systems in support of Defence Forces tasks. It is also responsible for coordinating all communications – radio and line – and information systems, communications research and updating of communications in line with modern developments and operational requirements. The CIS Corps is tasked with utilising networking and information technologies in order to dramatically increase Defence Force [[Organizational effectiveness|operational effectiveness]] through the provision of timely and accurate information to the appropriate commander, along with the real time efficient sharing of information and intelligence with the Army, Naval Service and Air Corps, as well as with multinational partners involved in international peacekeeping and other actors as required.<ref name="cis 1"/>

This role includes the development and maintenance of a secure nationwide Defence Forces Telecommunications Network (DFTN), which can support both protected voice and data services, and the provision and maintenance of [[Encryption|encrypted]] military communications equipment for use by Defence Forces personnel at home and abroad. CIS Corps units are dispersed throughout the DF giving Communications and IT support to each of the Army Brigades; Naval Service, Air Corps, [[Defence Forces Training Centre]] (DFTC) and Defence Forces Headquarters (DFHQ). The CIS Corps have Base Workshops where detailed maintenance, research and development is conducted.<ref name="cis 1"/>

The CIS Corps collar flash features the angel [[Gabriel]], the messenger of God, behind a signal shield and the caption ''"Cór Comharthaíochta"''. This is the Irish translation for 'Signals Corps', while the translation for Communications and Information Services Corps is ''"An Cór Seirbhísí Cumarsáide agus Eolais"''.<ref>{{cite web|title=An Cór Seirbhísí Cumarsáide agus Eolais|url=http://www.military.ie/ie/an-tarm/eagruchan/cor-an-airm/an-cor-cis/|publisher=Defence Forces Ireland|access-date=7 July 2015|archive-date=3 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150703124448/http://www.military.ie/ie/an-tarm/eagruchan/cor-an-airm/an-cor-cis/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Signals intelligence & cyber==
The Communications and Information Services (CIS) Corps works with the [[Irish Military Intelligence Service]] (IMIS), with regard to [[signals intelligence]] (SIGINT), and houses a dedicated SIGINT element within the Corps. The DF CIS Corps has the ability to intercept and monitor communications, remotely collect data, and process it.<ref>{{cite news|title=Military 'can help stop cyber attacks'|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/ireland/military-can-help-stop-cyber-attacks-313573.html|access-date=5 June 2015|publisher=The Irish Examiner|date=20 February 2015}}</ref> Under Irish legislation, the ''Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009'' and ''Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) Act 1993'' provides the Defence Forces with the legal authority to conduct domestic intelligence operations involving espionage, electronic communications and stored electronic information in order to safeguard and maintain the security of the state.<ref>{{cite web|title=Department of Defence: Defence Forces Intelligence Operations|url=http://www.kildarestreet.com/wrans/?id=2013-06-18a.42|work=18 June 2013|publisher=Kildare Street|access-date=8 February 2014}}</ref>

The CIS Corps along with the [[Garda Síochána]], the national police force, provide a significant domestic support role to the [[National Cyber Security Centre (Ireland)|National Cyber Security Centre]] (NCSC) of the [[Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration]] (formerly of the [[Department of Communications, Climate Action and Environment]]) in countering [[cyber-attack]]s, protecting [[critical infrastructure|critical national infrastructure]] and securing [[Government of Ireland|government]] communications.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Kennedy|first1=John|title=Ireland gears up for cyber war – new strategy to protect critical infrastructure|url=https://www.siliconrepublic.com/enterprise/2015/07/03/ireland-gears-up-for-cyber-war-new-strategy-to-protect-critical-infrastructure|access-date=12 July 2015|publisher=Silicon Republic|date=3 July 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=O'Brien|first1=Tim|title=Shatter launches debate on future of the Defence Forces|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/ireland/irish-news/shatter-launches-debate-on-future-of-the-defence-forces-1.1465472|access-date=5 June 2015|publisher=The Irish Times|date=16 July 2013}}</ref> CIS is responsible for cyber security within the Defence Forces, and maintains a capability in that area for the purpose of protecting its own networks and users domestic and foreign.<ref>{{cite web|title=National Cyber Security Strategy 2015-2017|url=http://www.dcenr.gov.ie/NR/rdonlyres/80C30B53-336F-45EF-9BDE-63F02A0E88C4/0/NationalCyberSecurityStrategy20152017.pdf|publisher=Department of Communications, Energy and Natural Resources|access-date=7 July 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150714150335/http://www.dcenr.gov.ie/NR/rdonlyres/80C30B53-336F-45EF-9BDE-63F02A0E88C4/0/NationalCyberSecurityStrategy20152017.pdf|archive-date=14 July 2015|df=dmy-all}}</ref> In 2016 the establishment of the Computer Incident Response Team (CIRT) in DFHQ CIS Company was revealed.<ref>{{cite web|title=Defence Forces Review 2015|url=http://www.military.ie/fileadmin/user_upload/images/Info_Centre/documents/Annual_Reviews/Defence_Forces_Review_2015.pdf|publisher=Defence Forces Ireland|access-date=24 September 2016}}</ref>

In July 2015, leaked email correspondence from ''[[Hacking Team]]'' – a private [[Italy|Italian]] spying and eavesdropping software company – reportedly showed members of the Irish CIS Corps in discussions with the company to purchase intrusion and surveillance "solutions" for the [[lawful interception]] of online communications, such as monitoring incoming and outgoing emails, browsing activity, [[Skype]] calls, remotely switching on webcams and microphones and remotely taking control of devices.<ref>{{cite news|last1=MacGuill|first1=Dan|title=Leaked emails show Irish Defence Forces held talks with controversial hacking company|url=https://www.thejournal.ie/irish-defence-forces-hacking-team-2206527-Jul2015/|access-date=9 July 2015|publisher=thejournal.ie|date=9 July 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Military chiefs: No software bought from hacker firm|url=http://www.independent.ie/business/technology/military-chiefs-no-software-bought-from-hacker-firm-31366035.html|access-date=10 July 2015|publisher=Irish Independent|date=10 July 2015}}</ref> A Defence Forces spokesperson said that for operational security reasons, it could not comment on specific elements of the activities of the CIS Corps, but confirmed that no goods or services were purchased from the company in question.<ref>{{cite news|title=Defence Forces emails leaked online - correspondence linked to controversial hacking company|url=http://www.rte.ie/news/2015/0709/713654-defence-forces-hacking/|access-date=9 July 2015|publisher=RTÉ News|date=9 July 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Lally|first1=Conor|title=Defence Forces emails to security firm leaked|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/crime-and-law/defence-forces-emails-to-security-firm-leaked-1.2279605|access-date=9 July 2015|publisher=The Irish Times|date=9 July 2015}}</ref>

The CIS Corps deployed '[[White hat (computer security)|ethical hackers]]' to fight back against the [[Health Service Executive ransomware attack]] in mid-2021, and sent CIS personnel to hospitals and HSE offices in order to decrypt devices affected by the cyberattack onsite. Reservists were particularly useful to this effort due to their cybersecurity skills and experience gleaned from the private sector.<ref>{{cite news |last1=O'Connor |first1=Niall |title=Defence Forces deployed 'ethical hackers' to fight back against massive HSE cyber attack |url=https://www.thejournal.ie/defence-forces-cis-how-they-fought-the-hse-cyber-attack-5499730-Jul2021/ |access-date=20 August 2021 |publisher=The Journal |date=20 July 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Cyber Security in the Defence Forces |url=https://play.acast.com/s/the-irish-defence-forces-podcast/s3ep10-cyber-security-in-the-defence-forces |access-date=20 August 2021 |publisher=Defence Forces Public Relations Branch |date=16 July 2021}}</ref>

==CIS School==
[[File:Nordic Battle Group ISTAR Training - CIS (5014802188).jpg|thumbnail|Irish Army CIS on [[Intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition, and reconnaissance|ISTAR]] training as part of the [[EU Battlegroup|EU]] [[Common Security and Defence Policy|CSDP]] [[Nordic Battlegroup]]]]
Soldiers join the Communications and Information Services Corps in one of the following apprenticeship trades;
*Communication Operative
*Electronic [[Engineering technician|Engineering Technician]]
*[[Software engineering|Software Engineering]] Technician
*[[Information systems technician|Information Technology Support Technician]]
*Communications & Information Services Technician
*Regimental [[Signaller]]
*Radio Instructor
*Telephone Maintenance Technician
*Data Communications Technician
*Microwave Systems Technician
*[[Network administrator|Network Administrator]]<ref name="cis 2">{{cite web|title=The CIS School|url=http://www.military.ie/en/education-hq/schools-of-the-dftc/cis-school/|publisher=Defence Forces Ireland|access-date=9 July 2015}}</ref>

All personnel do their basic military training.

The CIS School runs a large number of CIS related courses, including a degree programme in Military Communications for CIS technicians in association with the [[Institute of Technology, Carlow]].<ref name="cis 2"/>

There are 3 sections to the CIS School, providing training in the areas of operational procedures, technical proficiency and simulation.

'''Procedural and Operations Section''' ('''Proc/Ops''');
* Communications Operative Course
* Detachment Commanders Course
* [[Aerial rigging|Aerial Riggers]] Course
* Regimental Signals Course
* CIS Standard NCO Course
* CIS Young Officers Course

'''Technical Section''';
* CIS Trainee Technician Scheme (TTS)
* Technical Training Advancement Courses
* Strategic Applications Training

'''Simulation Section''';
* Digital Indoor Range Theatres (DIRT)
* [[Staff college|Command and Staff]] Trainer

The DIRT range is a digital [[Shooting range#Indoor|indoor shooting range]] in which trainees can be assessed on their marksmanship skills for the various [[small arms]] weapons used by the DF. It helps develop these proficiencies methodically without firing live ammunition on a regular basis.<ref name="cis 2"/> The €1 million facility is based at the [[Department of Defence (Ireland)|Department of Defence]] properties at [[Kilworth|Kilworth Camp]], [[County Cork]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Army sets its sights on €1m digital firing range at Kilworth camp|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/ireland/army-sets-its-sights-on-euro1m-digital-firing-range-at-kilworth-camp-279071.html|access-date=10 July 2015|publisher=The Irish Examiner|date=11 August 2014}}</ref>

===Retired units===
*4 Field CIS Company (4 FD CIS COY), [[Custume Barracks]], [[Athlone]]
*31 Reserve Field CIS Company (31 RES FD CIS COY), [[Sarsfield Barracks]], [[Limerick]] and [[Michael Collins (Irish leader)|Collins]] Barracks, Cork
*54 Reserve Field CIS Company (54 RES FD CIS COY), Custume Barracks, Athlone and Military Post, Sligo
*[[File:62CIS.svg|25px]] [[62 Res CIS Company|62 Reserve Field CIS Company]] (62 RES FD CIS COY), Cathal Brugha Barracks, Dublin
''The [[Reserve Defence Forces]] (RDF) units have been integrated with the Permanent Defence Forces (PDF) units as part of the "single force concept".''
